title: Nitroduck wants pollen to make more crops easier to edit
summary: Nitroduck wants pollen to make more crops easier to edit
body_markdown:
The hard part of editing a crop is not always deciding which trait to change. Getting from an edited cell to a viable plant can be a major obstacle.[Nitroduck](https://nitroduck.tech/) is developing a way around that step by using pollen to carry gene-editing machinery into the breeding process.


The Y Combinator Fall 2026 startup wants to make targeted changes more accessible across fruits and vegetables. Its proposed applications range from disease resistance to differences in color and flavor, with a broader goal of shortening the time breeders need to introduce new varieties.


At a high level, Nitroduck's approach is to deliver CRISPR through a pollen grain so that pollination can produce an edited seed. The attraction is compatibility with crossing plants, a process breeders already use, rather than requiring every new variety to pass through a difficult cell-to-plant regeneration workflow.


That is the company's proposed route to broader crop editing, not proof that it already works reliably in every crop. The launch does not provide crop-by-crop performance data, commercial release dates or evidence that the entire breeding and testing process has been reduced to a particular timeline.


[Watch Nitroduck's original launch video](https://youtu.be/Hi3vSHazXMk) .


The founders are Matej Zámečník, Matúš Grieš and Miroslav Rosputinský. Their earlier work offers a more concrete milestone than the company's sweeping crop ambitions: they helped lead the Brno team that won the Overgraduate Grand Prize at the 2025 iGEM synthetic-biology competition.


A[Masaryk University account](https://www.sci.muni.cz/clanky/cesti-a-slovensti-studenti-z-brna-ovladli-prestizni-celosvetovou-soutez-v-synteticke-biologii-igem) describes that team's work on duckweed, a small aquatic plant. The researchers initially wanted to improve its productivity, then focused on tools that made working with the plant easier. The resulting project included methods and equipment intended to speed up research.


That history explains Nitroduck's interest in the infrastructure behind crop development. A useful genetic idea has limited value to a breeder if introducing it into the desired plant remains slow or impractical. The startup is concentrating on that delivery problem, rather than announcing a single new fruit.


Its commercial argument is that faster development could make a wider range of traits worth pursuing. Disease resistance has an obvious agricultural purpose; flavor and appearance address a different customer, the person choosing produce. Nitroduck wants breeders to have more room to explore both.


The distinction between ambition and evidence remains important. Earlier duckweed work demonstrates relevant experience, but does not independently validate a pollen-based platform across different species. Likewise, an edited seed is a step toward a variety, not proof of field performance, market acceptance or authorization to sell it.


Nitroduck also describes reducing pesticide use as a long-term aim. That outcome would depend on the traits developed and how crops perform in practice. The public launch does not establish that pesticides can be eliminated or that resistance will remain effective indefinitely.


For breeders, the first meaningful result would be narrower: a reliable way to introduce a chosen trait into a variety they already want to cross. Nitroduck's proposed pollen route puts that practical hurdle ahead of the colorful produce pictured in its announcement.
